flashcards.q: What is the fixed review order and why does it matter?
flashcards.a: Correctness -> security -> design -> tests -> style. Each layer invalidates cheaper checks below it -- a wrong algorithm or a security hole makes design/style commentary on that code moot.

flashcards.q: What's the first command to run before reading a large PR's diff line by line?
flashcards.a: git diff --stat main...branch -- shows highest-churn files, which is usually where real logic lives, not the file with the most added lines (which may be a generated lockfile).

flashcards.q: What research underlies the ~200-400 line/hour and ~60-90 minute review-session guidance?
flashcards.a: The Cisco/SmartBear peer code review studies ("Best Kept Secrets of Peer Code Review") -- defect-detection effectiveness drops sharply past those thresholds, still cited unchanged in 2026 review guides.

flashcards.q: What's the actual test to determine if a unit test is meaningful, beyond "it passes"?
flashcards.a: Would flipping a real conditional or deleting a null check in the implementation make this specific test fail? If not, the test doesn't assert the behavior it claims to.

flashcards.q: What is an IDOR bug and where do you look for it in a diff?
flashcards.a: Insecure Direct Object Reference -- an endpoint checks the caller is logged in but not that the caller owns the specific resource ID requested. Check every handler taking a resource ID as a parameter for an ownership check tied to the authenticated caller.

flashcards.q: Why review tests before implementation code, and what's the risk of doing only that?
flashcards.a: Tests-first shows what behavior the author believes they built and highlights coverage gaps to focus on. Risk: it can bias your reading of the implementation toward the author's mental model instead of an independent read against real requirements.

flashcards.q: A test asserts `mock_transform.called_with(x)`. What's wrong with this as the sole assertion?
flashcards.a: It only proves a function was called with certain arguments, not that the transform produced correct output -- it asserts implementation interaction, not observable behavior.

flashcards.q: When is architectural pushback on a working, tested PR legitimate to block on, versus not?
flashcards.a: Legitimate when there's a concrete, stated future cost (duplicated logic that will drift, breaks testability of another module). Not legitimate when it's only "I'd have built it differently" with no identified cost -- that's a preference, not a blocker.

flashcards.q: Beyond "does the code using it work," what do you check for a new dependency in a PR?
flashcards.a: License compatibility, maintenance activity (last release/commit, open critical issues), transitive dependency footprint, and whether it duplicates a capability an existing dependency already provides.

flashcards.q: A shared utility used in 12 places is modified and all 12 callers' existing tests pass. Is that sufficient?
flashcards.a: Only if those tests actually exercise the specific behavior that changed -- weak coverage at a call site can pass every existing test while still breaking that call site's real production behavior.
